🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase**.

From **August 2009** to **June 2012**, Matt served as Technology Delivery Lead for ACCESS Next Generation, the bank’s global corporate banking portal. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided the foundation, but the bank needed payment modules, security controls, and workflows beyond its out-of-box capabilities. Regional systems had different data models, payment formats, and regulatory requirements, while corporate administrators were spending days manually configuring user permissions.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, determining where native platform capabilities ended and bespoke engineering was required.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules. That included NACHA file validation, integration with the bank’s foreign exchange engine, and a Message Authentication Code security layer for verifying payment integrity before release. He also delivered the centralized payments gateway: message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**, replacing fragmented point-to-point integrations.

For administrators, Matt introduced bulk permission changes across users, accounts, and products from a single screen, plus payment-type-specific controls, such as allowing wire approval without FX initiation. Entitlement management dropped from **days to minutes**.

He led payments data migration without disruption to live payment operations and mapped regional compliance requirements into data visibility and access controls. Rather than a single big-bang deployment, rollout sequencing followed regulatory readiness across APAC, EMEA, and the Americas. He also owned on-call and critical production incident response.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a unified portal serving **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. The gateway gave corporate treasurers a single entry point for wire, ACH, and cross-border transfers across regions.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership philosophy.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. He builds a “permit to fail” learning environment and brings Product, Engineering, and Design together in balanced teams.

Many teams he inherited were over-processed, under-trusted, and waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes. His focus was to remove those barriers: make intent explicit, create psychological safety so people could speak honestly, and push decisions to the people closest to the work. He coached teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, that meant assembling engineers, product managers, and UX architects with equal participation and shared accountability. Matt aligned team goals with client and business outcomes, embedded pair programming and collaborative coding, and used stand-ups, retrospectives, and knowledge-sharing sessions to identify roadblocks. Teams could voice feedback and implement changes autonomously rather than wait for approval.

When fear of blame discouraged experimentation, Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems and supported lean, low-stakes experiments. He emphasized lessons learned rather than pointing fingers. In product incubation, he set expectations upfront that prototypes and user tests would sometimes fail, then helped teams use those results to shape product direction week by week.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** once they embraced lean product and modern engineering practices. Balanced teams also achieved **zero-defect production code** through iterative development and real-time feedback loops.

🐾 Here’s what Matt has built, changed, and delivered.

Matt’s work centers on execution and delivery, organization transformation, and talent development. He has built enterprise platforms and the engineering organization that delivers them, from engineer to Director, including payments and banking modernization at **JP Morgan Chase**, **RBC**, **Capital One**, and **HSBC**.

At **Accenture**, clients wanted to move away from waterfall delivery, feature factories, and siloed teams. They needed modern engineering practices that could work alongside legacy systems, compliance requirements, and enterprise governance. Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, owning full P&L accountability, hiring, training, and development across engineering, architecture, product, and design.

Instead of separating product, design, and engineering through handoffs, he established balanced teams working together. He embedded pair programming, test-driven development, automated pipelines, and customer journey-led development. New practitioners progressed through an “I do, we do, you do” learning model, with tailored training and experienced mentors. The talent program achieved near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**.

At **Capital One**, slow, misaligned product iterations were extending time-to-market. Matt introduced a client-prioritized, testable backlog and disciplined red-green-refactor practice within an **8-person** cross-functional team. They delivered features **3 to 4x faster** than other **Accenture** teams on the same engagement, with **zero production defects**. The client sought to retain the team beyond its planned end.

Across the Cloud Innovation Centers, teams achieved **4X faster velocity**, with **10-person** balanced teams delivering equivalent output to traditional **20-person** teams. The centers delivered **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune 500 clients** and contributed to **\$100M+ in repeatable business** through delivery excellence, client advocacy, and repeat engagements.

answer_md:
🐾 Matt’s example is a platform delivery where he assumed safety controls were correct instead of verifying them.

He was the tech lead on a global platform modernization for a financial services client, with dev, QA, UAT, and production environments. The program was under delivery pressure, and offshore teams were executing test cycles across environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on that documentation without confirming its accuracy. He focused on delivery pressures rather than validating access patterns, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not implement compensating controls such as data masking or email interception. He also did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed, then worked collectively to implement corrective controls. The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project, a systemic failure with an individual consequence.

Matt’s stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.
